title: Chosen from a Shortlist: Kure and Its Naval Century
standfirst: In 1883 the navy's surveyors quietly measured a fishing bay against three rival sites. Once Kure won, the navy took half of one village's land, built the port that launched the battleship Yamato, and for a time after 1945 commanded occupying Australian and British forces from here. This dossier reads the fishing village underneath the fleet base.

paragraphs.text: Before the navy came, Kure was a small farming and fishing settlement on Aki Bay, one of several villages the Meiji navy quietly compared against each other. In February 1883 the Navy Hydrographic Department sent Lieutenant Commander Kimotsuki and Lieutenant Miura to survey Kure Bay and the waters nearby; Tokuyama, Mihara and the island of Etajima were also candidates for what would become the navy's Second District headquarters. A district history published in 1943 recalls that rumors of the survey alone unsettled a village that, as yet, knew nothing of the navy. On 14 July 1884 Prince Arisugawa Takehito, with the navy minister and other senior officers, came in person to inspect Kure Bay and its shore; once the survey confirmed it as the best of the candidates, orders went out to begin buying land.

The following year the choice was sealed in public. On 4 August 1885, during a tour of Yamaguchi and Hiroshima prefectures, Emperor Meiji sailed into Kure Bay escorted by the warship Kasuga, walked the deck to view the future naval port's site for himself, and was told in detail why it had been chosen; villagers who lined the shore, the same history records, wept at the sight of the imperial ship passing far out on the water.

Buying the land took several rounds of negotiation between 1884 and 1888, led in turn by a changing cast of naval officers. It fell hardest on Miyahara, the village whose fields and house lots covered the ground the new town would actually occupy: the navy eventually took half of Miyahara's roughly 153 cho of farmland and residential land, and the 1943 history says plainly that the village saw a change 'nearly amounting to its total destruction.' The neighboring villages of Washo and Shoyamada lost every part of their land that faced the sea, though Washo kept some houses and Shoyamada, being newer reclaimed ground, had only a handful of households to move. The same source records the compensation paid per unit of land: at most a little over 170 yen for the best paddy fields, as little as 50 yen for poor dry fields, and up to 200 yen for house plots, figures that meant something very different to a farming household than to the navy drawing up its budget.

Before the port existed, official visitors simply lodged with local people. The 1943 history notes that Kimotsuki, the officer who surveyed the bay in 1883, and Maki, who came to arrange land purchases in 1885, both stayed at a commoner's house near the bay called the Ebisuya; later dignitaries, including the future prime minister Ito Hirobumi and the navy minister who attended the port's opening ceremony, lodged at a private house in Wada village for lack of anything grander. The first sailors transferred from Yokosuka in 1889 landed from a merchant ship at Kawarishi and were put up at an inn called the Akamatsuya, a measure of how little of a naval town existed yet even as the chinjufu itself opened for business.

The paperwork that mattered most was signed on 28 May 1889, when a naval ordinance formally placed the Second Naval District's chinjufu, or naval district headquarters, at Kure, alongside Yokosuka and Sasebo. Its first commander, Nakamuta, sailed in and took up his post on 22 June that year; because the old chinjufu system was being reorganized at the same moment, his arrival ceremony was combined with the base's own opening. Two sources consulted for this dossier, one from 1935 and one from 1943, both date the chinjufu's formal opening ceremony to the following year, 1890, suggesting the base was already at work for months before it was ceremonially declared open.

What followed was explosive growth. Kure counted around 39,600 people in 1898; by the time it was incorporated as a city on 1 October 1902, under its first mayor, Sakuma Giichiro, it had 13,809 households and 60,132 residents, and its own household registers for that year show more people living there as temporary migrants than as locally registered residents. The merger that created the city was itself pushed through in a single afternoon: the prefectural governor sailed to Kure on 26 January 1902, met some sixty local representatives at Myohoji temple, and argued that a naval arsenal town competing for a planned national steelworks could not afford four separate village administrations for its water, schools, roads and fire brigades.

The years around the chinjufu's opening turned a construction site into a town in a hurry. A telegraph line to Hiroshima was under construction by 1886 and running by the next year; a straight new road ran from the naval gate through Washo, with further roads pushed out to Yoshiura, Aga, Hiro, Miyahara and Kego-ya; steamers began calling at Kawarishi; the Aki district government office moved to Kure from Kaita in April 1887; and elementary schools, a red-light district at Yoshiura and a bathing resort all opened within a few years of each other. The military and civilian sides of the new town marked their new relationship in person: on New Year's Day 1888 some 120 people, naval officers down to the chinjufu's chief surgeon and paymaster, county officials and the heads of the three villages, gathered for the first joint New Year's party at a restaurant in Wada village, an occasion the 1943 history calls the start of official-and-civilian goodwill in the port town.

War, when it came, brought the imperial family to Kure in person. During the war with China, Emperor Meiji sailed into the naval port on 2 October 1894, lunched at the chinjufu, inspected the warships Hiei and Saikyo-maru, handed out sake to their crews and sent an envoy to console the wounded at the naval hospital; the crown prince followed on 19 November, watching net-fishing near the coal depot before his own hospital visit and a tour of the shipyard; the Empress came in her turn on 30 March 1895, going directly from the chinjufu to the naval hospital to see the wounded. The same years saw the port's first full-scale naval exercise, in 1891, fought out across the straits and hills around nearby Nomi Island and Miyajima with a mock headquarters, coastal gun positions and a field hospital, a rehearsal for the war that would follow within the decade.

By 1935 a city guidebook could call Kure one of Japan's ten largest cities, with about 230,000 people and, in its own words, the Orient's greatest naval port, able to berth more than sixty warships of the Combined Fleet at once. The Naval Arsenal's own workforce had already lived through one full boom and bust: it passed 30,000 workers at the height of the 'Eight-Eight Fleet' building program in the early 1920s, collapsed almost overnight when the Washington Naval Treaty capped Japan's fleet, and by the mid-1930s was climbing again as international tension returned.

The Arsenal's best-known product was the battleship Yamato, completed there on 16 December 1941: 263 meters long, 38.9 meters at the beam, with a standard displacement of 65,000 tons, the largest battleship ever built. It survived barely three and a half years of war. Sent out on a one-way mission toward Okinawa with fuel for only a single voyage, Yamato was sunk by American carrier aircraft on 7 April 1945, taking most of her crew down with her.

Kure itself came under direct attack in the war's last year. Library reference sources tracing the city's air-raid record list American attacks on 4 May, 21 June and 1 July 1945, and a further raid on 24 July in which the cruiser Tone, moored in the harbor, came under sustained anti-aircraft fire from around 8:40 in the morning; the wider raids on Hiroshima Prefecture ran from November 1944 to within days of the war's end. Weeks earlier, on 30 March 1945, American B-29s had already sown naval mines across the waters around Kure and Hiroshima as part of a wider campaign to seal the Inland Sea.

The worst single blow, though, fell after the fighting stopped. On 17 September 1945, little more than a month after the surrender, the Makurazaki Typhoon tore through the ruined city: a monument raised afterward records 1,154 dead and 1,162 houses swept away across Kure, with 309 of the dead in Miyahara alone, the same district the navy had half-demolished sixty years before to build the port in the first place. A second flood disaster, in July 1967, killed a further 88 people in the city, 14 of them again in Miyahara, a reminder that the hills hemming in Kure's narrow waterfront make the city as vulnerable to landslides and flash floods as it once was strategically valuable.

Defeat brought a different kind of occupation. The British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) — troops from Britain, India, New Zealand and Australia, about 45,000 in all, of whom roughly 16,000 were Australian — landed its main body at Kure on 21 February 1946 and made the former naval port its headquarters, administering Hiroshima, Shimane, Yamaguchi, Tottori and Okayama prefectures and Shikoku on the Allied occupation's behalf. A history of Hiroshima Prefecture's police records that Commonwealth troops based at Kure used an army training ground further inland for exercises from September 1946. The former Imperial Naval Academy on the nearby island of Etajima became the occupying force's general headquarters, its full facilities put to work running the occupation and employing thousands of Japanese laborers; a photograph reproduced in the city's own official history shows some of them building a pumping station for the Commonwealth headquarters there on 26 November 1947, after the base ran short of water.

The clearest place to take in this whole arc is the Yamato Museum, opened on 23 April 2005 as the city's own maritime history museum, built around a large one-tenth-scale model of the battleship; it drew a million visitors within its first 177 days and had passed fifteen million by 2022. A short walk away, the wooded grounds of the former Kure Naval District commander-in-chief's official residence survive as the Irifuneyama Memorial Hall, now a museum of decorative gilt paper, with the Arsenal's old clock tower still standing on the same grounds.

The city's own present-day account of itself leads with the same history, describing Kure as a 'Japan Heritage city' before almost anything else. Kure and the three other original chinjufu towns, Yokosuka, Sasebo and Maizuru, are grouped today under a single Japan Heritage designation telling the story of how Meiji Japan built naval defenses at four natural harbors to hold its own against the Western powers, a story whose surviving pieces in Kure include the old headquarters buildings, the shipyard where Yamato was built, and wartime gun emplacements on the surrounding hills. Those same hills, steep and close to the water, are the other half of the story: the district's own disaster memorials, most recently one recording three deaths in a debris flow at Yoshiura in the heavy rains of July 2018, mark a hazard that has run alongside Kure's naval history for its entire century and a half.

timeline.what: Navy surveyors examine Kure Bay as a candidate site for a new naval district headquarters.
Prince Arisugawa Takehito personally inspects Kure Bay; land purchases begin soon after.
Emperor Meiji sails into Kure Bay to view the future naval port's site.
Land is bought from Miyahara, Washo and Shoyamada villages in stages; Miyahara loses about half its farmland and house lots.
A naval ordinance formally places the Second Naval District's chinjufu at Kure.
The chinjufu's first commander, Nakamuta, arrives and takes up his post.
Two later sources date the chinjufu's formal opening ceremony to this year.
Kure is incorporated as a city, with Sakuma Giichiro as its first mayor; population has already passed 60,000.
The battleship Yamato is completed at Kure Naval Arsenal.
American mine-laying and repeated air raids strike Kure, including an attack on the cruiser Tone on 24 July.
Yamato is sunk by American carrier aircraft en route to Okinawa.
The Makurazaki Typhoon kills 1,154 people in Kure, 309 of them in Miyahara.
The main body of the British Commonwealth Occupation Force -- troops from Britain, India, New Zealand and Australia -- lands at Kure and makes the former naval port its headquarters.
The Yamato Museum opens in Kure.

walk.name: Yamato Museum
walk.what: Kure's own maritime history museum, built around a large-scale model of the battleship Yamato; opened 2005 and now visited by well over a million people a year.

walk.name: Irifuneyama Memorial Hall
walk.what: The former official residence of the Kure Naval District's commanders-in-chief, set in wooded grounds that also keep the old Naval Arsenal's clock tower.

walk.name: Miyahara
walk.what: The village that lost half its land to the naval port in the 1880s and 309 people to the Makurazaki Typhoon in 1945; today part of central Kure, with little visible trace of the farming settlement it once was.

walk.name: The Arsenal waterfront
walk.what: The shipyards and dockside where the Yamato and thousands of other naval vessels were built, still in industrial use and best viewed from the Yamato Museum's harbor-facing windows and walkways.

walk.name: Yoshiura
walk.what: A hillside district on the western edge of the old naval-port land takings, and the site of fatal debris flows in the heavy rains of July 2018, a reminder of the terrain that shaped the port as much as the navy did.

caveats: Two sources used here (from 1935 and 1943) both date the Kure chinjufu's formal opening ceremony to 1890, a year after the naval ordinance that created it (28 May 1889) and the arrival of its first commander (22 June 1889); this dossier reports both dates rather than resolving the apparent gap on its own authority.

This dossier's BCOF facts are checked against the Australian War Memorial's own account, reached directly in this session, for the force's arrival date, total strength and the prefectures it administered. Japanese library and archive sources (via the Collaborative Reference Database) supply the remaining detail used here: Commonwealth troops' use of an inland training ground from September 1946, and Japanese laborers' work for the force at Etajima. The Department of Veterans' Affairs' Anzac Portal returned a server error and could not be checked; BCOF's full command structure beyond its four contributing countries is not stated here because it could not be verified.

The exact construction date of the Irifuneyama commander-in-chief's residence, and the exact year of Kure's Japan Heritage designation, could not be confirmed from the official pages read this session and are therefore not stated.

Casualty figures for the 1945 and 1967 disasters and the 2018 Yoshiura debris flow come from this project's own disaster-memorial dataset (drawn from the Geospatial Information Authority's Natural Disaster Legacy Monuments register) rather than from a source independently read in full this session.
